OSCAR SENTENCING PROCEDURE

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
This week,in the same court that Oscar Pistorius stood trial,he will have to face prosecutor Gerrie Nel and Judge Masipa again.Only this time,the prospect of a much longer sentence hangs over his head

Summary:
This week, in the same court that Oscar Pistorius stood trial, he will have to face chief prosecutor Gerrie Nel and Judge Masipa again. Only this time, the prospect of a much longer sentence hangs over his head.
During the sentencing procedure, adv Gerrie Nel will call witnesses in aqggravation of Pistorius's sentence, while adv Barry Roux will call witnesses in mitigation of his sentence.


Further information:
It is not the first time that this process is being followed. In October 2014, Judge Masipa sentenced Oscar Pistorius to five years in prison according to section 276 (1)(i) of the Criminal Procedures Act - which meant that in Oscar's case he had to serve 10 months of his five year sentence - one fifth according to the section he was sentenced to.

He was supposed to be released on the 21st of August last year, but Minister of Justice found a techical error in the law and he was only released in October, one year less than a year from the date he first entered the Kgosi Mampuru II prison in Pretoria.

Not long after - in November 2015 - Gerrie Nel brought his application at the Supreme Court of Appeal to have Judge Masipa's verdict of culpable homicide changed to murder. And in December 2015, in an unanimous judgment - written and read by Chief Justice Eric Leach - the verdict was changed to murder - Oscar Pistorius's must have foreseen that by firing four shots through the toilet cubicle he would have killed the person behind the door and therefore he was guilty of murder.

And that is why we find ourselves at the High Court in Pretoria again now - two years and three months after Oscar Pistorius's initial trial started.

It is likely that court will sit the entire week - chief prosecutor Gerrie Nel and adv Barry Roux will call their respective witnesses to testify in aggravation and mitigation of his sentence and then the two legal heads still has to deliver their final arguments.
It is then likely that Judge Masipa will postpone the case to deliberate her sentence.

2. Willem Pretorius (cameraman) and his assistent (Jared) daily fee for 3 days as he had to be booked for 5 days - 2 of those days will be paid by Este as per normal story arrangement

Press Release:


Oscar Pistorius Sentencing
This week, Reeva Steenkamp’s father, 73-year-old Barry, told the North Gauteng High Court in Pretoria that he felt like his daughter’s murder on Valentine’s Day 2013 happened ‘yesterday’. It’s been over three years since shamed athlete Oscar Pistorius shot and killed Reeva, his then girlfriend. In December last year the Supreme Court of Appeal overturned the original culpable homicide verdict handed down to him by the High Court, to a verdict of murder. This week the second round of arguments in mitigation and aggravation of sentence saw the case once again dominate global headlines. Carte Blanche brings key analysis to these proceedings.


Script:


OSCAR SENTENCING SCRPT

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK

PRESENTER: JOHN WEBB

BROADCAST DATE: 19 JUNE 2016

“No words can adequately capture my feelings about the devastating accident that has caused such heartache for everyone who truly loved – and continues to love Reeva.
The pain and sadness – especially for Reeva’s parents, family and friends - consumes me with sorrow.”

Words of regret from Oscar Pistorius posted on his website exactly a year after he shot and killed Reeva Steenkamp at his Pretoria home.
In March 2014, he stood trial in the North Gauteng High Court on a charge of murder. He was found not guilty of murder, but instead convicted of culpable homicide.

In December 2015, the state succesfully appealed this verdict and in a unanimous judgment the Supreme Court of Appeal found Oscar guilty of dolus eventualis – murder with indirect intent.

[CB 6 DECEMBER 2015/JUSTICE ERIC LEACH]: One does really not know what his explanation is having fired the fatal shots. I have no doubt that in firing the fatal shots the accused must have foreseen and therefore did foresee that whoever was behind the toilet door, might die, but reconciled himself to that event occurring and gambled with that person's life.

Retired Judge Chris Greenland, advocate, Mannie Witz and attorney Michael Motsoeneng-Bill all followed the trial closely as commentators.

JUDGE GREENLAND: Judge Masipa has an unenviable task here. You succeed as a court and as a judge if at the end of the trial human beings are satisfied justice has been done and seen to be done.

MANNIE WITZ: If I was the judge, I would definitely take into accounts the sentiments, the decision of the SCA, you must take into account the one year that he has already sat.

JOHN LINK: Barry Steenkamp shunned the spotlight during the trial, but felt that he had to testify in aggravation of sentence. He conceded that his wife June had forgiven Oscar but says that he thinks about Reeva every moment of every day and says that Oscar has to pay a price.

BARRY STEENKAMP: People say it takes you two year, three years and you start to feel a little bit better about the whole thing. But everyday of my life is the same.

Barry testified he had almost become a recluse since Reeva’s death.

BARRY STEENKAMP: I don’t wish that on anyone human being, finding out what happened.

He says he’s haunted by what Reeva must have gone through during the last moments of her life.

BARRY STEENKAMP: She must have been in so much fear and pain – that is what I think of it all the time. I visualize that I can see it myself.

GERRIE NEL: Because of that, you also tried to hurt yourself?

BARRY STEENKAMP: I thought the pain that Reeva went through, I used to just – I don’t know whether I was going mental or whatever – I used to take my fist and hit it against the walls, my knuckles – my injection from my diabetes, I used to take the needle and shove it into my stomach and arms to see if I could feel the same type of pain, but no…

Oscar’s defence advocate Barry Roux and chief state prosecutor, Gerrie Nel each called three witnesses.
As they gave evidence inside a packed courtroom, the Paralympian sat in the accused’s dock looking dazed and forlorn.

PROF SCHOLTZ: He has become despondent, lethargic and disinvested – leaving his future in the hands of God.

Oscar was described as “an ill and broken man” by the defence’s first and primary witness, psychologist Professor Jonathan Scholtz.
He was part of the clinical team who examined Oscar when he was sent to Weskoppies Psychiatric Hospital for observation during his 2014 trial.
Earlier this month, he did a further assessment to determine Oscar’s current state of mind.

PROF SCHOLTZ: My opinion is his current condition warrants hospitilisation.

[SENTENCING DAY 1] JOHN LINK: Professor Scholtz believes Oscar’s conditions has deteriorated since he first evaluated him in 2014. He says the athlete is suffering from the serious depression, post traumatic stress and anxiety. In fact, he says Oscar’s condition is so severe that he is unable to testify in mitigation of sentence.

PROFESSOR SCHOLTZ: For his own protection, he was segregated in an area of the hospital ward, Unfortunately, this effectively amounted to solitary confinement. He was confined to his cell for at least 18 hours per day of which the psychological experience was that of being caged like an animal.
But during cross-examination, chief prosecutor Gerrie Nel said Oscar had, in his sessions with Scholtz, been untruthful about certain scenarios.

GERRIE NEL: Mr Pistorius was not confined to his cell.

PROF SCHOLTZ: He explained to me it wasn’t every day all the time, there were instances where he was allowed more freedom.

GERRIE NEL: His cell, where he was kept in, was open during the day. He could move in the section where he was kept.

PROF SCHOLTZ: I understand that, my Lady, the fear however, of coming to some harm made him confine himself to his bed most of the time. Somebody did came through to the section and assaulted him there. I confimed this with his psychotherapist who saw him over the next day or two, but …

GERRIE NEL: I will lead evidence that according to the complaints register that’s just not true. It’s a lie.

Assistant health manager at the Kgosi Mampuru II Prison, sister Charlotte Mashabane, who testified for the state in aggravation of sentence denied this claim.

SISTER CHARLOTTE MASHABANE: We don’t have any report of being assaulted in..

GERRIE NEL: If it happened, would you have known about it?

CHARLOTTE MASHABANE: Yes.

Professor Scholtz testified that Oscar was traumatised by seeing the body of a fellow inmate who committed suicide.

PROF. SCHOLTZ: He explained to me that he was hanging in the door frame for quite a period of time.

But Mashabane testified the suicide took place in another ward to which Oscar wouldn’t have had access to without supervision.

Mashabane described three incidents relating to her medical treatment in which Oscar lost his temper during the first six months of his incarceration.

GERRIE NEL: Did he say something about your competance, even dr. Tsatse’s competance?

CHARLOTTE MASHABANE: He talked about dr. Tsatse, even ourselves, that we are being so useless, not knowledgeble.

Professor Scholtz testified that Oscar showed remorse and that Oscar had admitted to him that he shot through the bathroom door intentionally.

DR. SCHOLTZ: He accepts he took a human life when he shouldn’t have.

GERRIE NEL: Did mr Pistorius indicate to you that he intentionally shot at the door, knowing there was a person in the bathroom?

DR. SCHOLTZ: Yes, if you put it like that, he did.

GERRIE NEL: That is the first version of him intentionally shooting that we’ve had in this court.

JOHN LINK: The upshot of a fairly lengthy submission by Prof Scholtz was that any further time behind bars for Oscar Pistorius would be detrimental. During his cross-examination, Gerrie Nel painted Scholtz as a biased witness.

MICHAEL: whether the bias was to such a nature that what he was saying can be discounted – I don’t think so.

JUDGE GREENLAND: he admitted that he was only talking to the interests of the accused. It gave me, if I was the judge, a very clear picture of the real life situation of the person I now have to sentence.

On Wednesday morning, the state called it’s final witness in aggravation of sentence – Reeva’s cousin, Kim Martin. She also testified when Oscar was sentenced for culpable homicide.

KIM MARTIN: Not a day goes by without thinking about her. The scars, the effects, runs very, very deep. All we’ve ever wanted is the truth. I never, ever heard him say I apologise for shooting and murdering Reeva behind that door.

In June Steenkamp’s book, A Mother’s Story, released in 2014 she wrote: “As long as we live, as long as breathe, Barry and I will struggle to come to terms with Reeva’s death. We are locked in unbearable grief forever.”

BARRY STEENKAMP: A lot of people have said that June is this stone-faced person, does she actually feel or whatever. I know that June grieves like I do all the time. She is most probably a bit stronger, but she grieves. I hear her at night, I hear her cry.

In advocate Barry Roux’s closing arguments, he argued that Judge Masipa should consider whether the threat of an attack was subjectively perceived to be real at the time of the offence.

JOHN LINK: The central theme in Roux’s closing arguments is his believe that some in society still confuse dolus eventualis with dolus directus – with other words, despite the findings of the Supreme Court of Appeal, some people still mistakenly, perhaps even willfully believe that Oscar intended to shoot Reeva Steenkamp.

BARRY ROUX: We say, my Lady, that as the result as a sustained campaign of misonformation, the accused’s reputation will never recover.

JOHN LINK: Roux went on to argue that some members of society appears unable to reconcile their image of Oscar as the medal-winning athlete standing 1,84 metres on his blades with the anxious man standing 1,5 metres on his stumps, who on the morning of the shooting believed that his life was in danger.

BARRY ROUX: Some people refuse point-black to see in context the true facts. They want to see Oscar Pistorius running to the bathroom with his gold medal around his neck.

JUDGE GREENLAND: He addressed society and lambasted it and scolded it. In my 35 years in the court I’ve never seen this but I cant fault Barry for doing it.

In an unexpected move, advocate Roux asked Oscar to remove his prosthetic legs. On his stumps, Oscar walked past Reeva’s family and the prosecution team and then stood in front of Judge Masipa, with his head bowed.

BARRY ROUX: Let’s look at who is the person. After incorporating the Supreme Court of Appeal’s finding to view the sentence. He was suffering from an anxiety disorder, that is not gone. This must all be seen in the context of his disability and the pervasive effect of the disability on his subjective thinking. I don’t want to overplay disability, but at time has come that we must just look with different eyes, at least with unbiased eyes.

MANNIE WITZ: I think the visual reminder is very important. Any prociding officer, when you actually see it, one or two minutes of actually seeing it, is better than an hour explaining it

JUDGE GREENLAND: Oscar is still a human being judge Masipa has to also protect his interest, and she was put into a better position to do so by that visual impact of seeing him on his stumps.

According to the Criminal Procedures Act, murder carries a minimum sentence of 15 years imprisonment unless substantial and compelling circumstances exist.

MANNIE WITZ: You can just see Oscar, as this trial has progressed, look at him now, nevermind that he now faces the minimum sentence, he is a broken man

BARRY ROUX: The accused has paid from the minute he fired the shots and will pay for this for the rest of his life.

Roux has asked the court for a sentence of correctional supervision. Professor Scholtz testified that further imprisonment would serve no constructive purpose for Oscar.

In prosecutor Gerrie Nel’s closing arguments he emphasizes that the benchmark for murder is a minimum of 15 years.

GERRIE NEL: Correctional supervision is not even close to the benchmark.

JOHN LINK:Nel turned immediately to an issue covered extensively by Barry Roux in his closing arguments. He acknowledged that the SCA had found Oscar guilty of murder dolus eventualis, but said this shooting was far removed from negligence.

GERRIE NEL: At the time the fatal shots were fired, the possibility of death of the person behind the door was a clear and obvious result, and infiring not one, but four shots, such a result become even more likely. My Lady, more likely than obvious. My Lady, it borders on Dolus Directus, not on negligence, My Lady.

JOHN LINK: Throughout sentencing, Nel referred to a television interview that Oscar had taken part in prior to these proceedings. He said in doing so, and in not choosing to testify in mitigation of sentence had shown disrespect for the court. He also accused Oscar of showing no remorse.

MANNIE WITZ: The defence laid down a proper basis from the evidence of Prof Scholtz why he couldn’t actually give the evidence to express the remorse, when you give evidence in mitigation of sentence or extentuation of sentence, you can be cross-examined and you can be cross-examined on the very merits of the case.

GERRIE NEL: My Lady, there is a difference: “I am very sorry that Reeva is dead,” and “I feel sorry for myself because she is dead.” That I understand. But, my Lady, why? In the light of these contradictions one really does not know what his explanation is for firing the fatal shots. My Lady, that in itself, excludes remorse.

JUDGE GREENLAND: He owes the court an explanation. He owes society an explanation, he owes the Steenkamps an explanation, especially on that critical issue as to what was his intention when he fired those shots. I think the SCA has lamented the fact that is still unanswered.

GERRIE NEL: Life was the most valuable asset of the deceased. My Lady, it does not matter if the accused thought she was an intruder. Is an intruder’s life not important? Did he not think of an intruder’s life? He didn’t. He intentionally, in his view, on the argument of the defence, intentionally killed an intruder. That’s not important. As long as we can just cover in our argument that he never though he was killing Reeva, then we’re covered.

Prosecutor Gerrie Nel asked that Judge Masipa do not deviate from the prescribed minimum 15-year imprisonment for murder.

JUDGE GREENLAND: The sentence that I would impose is one of 15 years house arrest. Where house arrest means house imprisonment. In other words no liberties except liberties within his home environment, coupled with 15 years of community service

MANNIE: I think it would probably be an effective term of imprisonment in these circumstances.

Judge Masipa will hand down her sentence on July, the 6th.

Barry said that he believed that one day he’d be able to meet with Oscar.

BARRY STEENKAMP: It’s been very difficult for me to forgive, but he has to pay for his crime.



PROMO’S

PROMO 1:15”
BARRY STEENKAMP: People say it takes two, three years to get over something like this. But everyday of my life is the same.

A broken Barry Steenkamp says Oscar Pistorius has to pay for what he’s done.


PROMO 2:15”
BARRY ROUX: Let’s let at who is this man – with unbiased eyes.

PROF. SCHOLTZ: one would describe him as “broken”.

Barry Steenkamp, a broken man himself, says Oscar must pay for what he’s done.

BARRY STEENKAMP: It’s been very difficult for me to forgive.


PROMO 3:10”
It’s been three years and four months since Oscar Pistorius shot and killed his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp. Now convicted of murder, he was back in court this week for sentencing proceedings.























This week, though, the court was given a direct insight into the “devastation” Oscar wrote about , from Reeva’s father, Barry Steenkamp.

Words of loss and sympathy – written by Oscar Pistorius and posted on his website exactly one year after he shot and killed his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp on Valentine’s day 2013.


But another distraught and broken man, sometimes even at a loss for words, was Reeva’s father, Barry Steenkamp, who testified in aggravation of sentence for the first time this week.

But the Appeal Court also ruled that despite Oscar maintaining that he believed there was in intruder, “the identity of his victim is irrelevant to his guilt”.

PROF SCHOLTZ: He explained to me it wasn’t every day all the time, there were instances where he was allowed more freedom. GERRIE NEL: His cell, where he was kept in, was open during the day. He could move in the section where he was kept. PROF SCHOLTZ: I understand that, my Lady, the fear however, of coming to some harm made him confine himself to his bed most of the time. Somebody did came through to the section and assaulted him there. I confimed this with his psychotherapist who saw him over the next day or two, but … GERRIE NEL: I will lead evidence that according to the complaints register that’s just not true. It’s a lie. Assistant health manager at the Kgosi Mampuru II Prison, sister Charlotte Mashabane, who testified for the state in aggravation of sentence denied this claim. SISTER CHARLOTTE MASHABANE: We don’t have any report of being assaulted in.. GERRIE NEL: If it happened, would you have known about it? CHARLOTTE MASHABANE: Yes. Professor Scholtz testified that Oscar was traumatised by seeing the body of a fellow inmate who committed suicide. PROF. SCHOLTZ: He explained to me that he was hanging in the door frame for quite a period of time. But Mashabane testified the suicide took place in another ward to which Oscar wouldn’t have had access to without supervision. Mashabane described three incidents relating to her medical treatment in which Oscar lost his temper during the first six months of his incarceration. GERRIE NEL: Did he say something about your competance, even dr. Tsatse’s competance? CHARLOTTE MASHABANE: He talked about dr. Tsatse, even ourselves, that we are being so useless, not knowledgeble. Professor Scholtz testified that Oscar showed remorse and that Oscar had admitted to him that he shot through the bathroom door intentionally. DR. SCHOLTZ: He accepts he took a human life when he shouldn’t have. GERRIE NEL: Did mr Pistorius indicate to you that he intentionally shot at the door, knowing there was a person in the bathroom? DR. SCHOLTZ: Yes, if you put it like that, he did. GERRIE NEL: That is the first version of him intentionally shooting that we’ve had in this court. JOHN LINK: The upshot of a fairly lengthy submission by Prof Scholtz was that any further time behind bars for Oscar Pistorius would be detrimental. During his cross-examination, Gerrie Nel painted Scholtz as a biased witness. MICHAEL: whether the bias was to such a nature that what he was saying can be discounted – I don’t think so. JUDGE GREENLAND: he admitted that he was only talking to the interests of the accused. It gave me, if I was the judge, a very clear picture of the real life situation of the person I now have to sentence. On Wednesday morning, the state called it’s final witness in aggravation of sentence – Reeva’s cousin, Kim Martin. She also testified when Oscar was sentenced for culpable homicide. KIM MARTIN: Not a day goes by without thinking about her. The scars, the effects, runs very, very deep. All we’ve ever wanted is the truth. I never, ever heard him say I apologise for shooting and murdering Reeva behind that door. In June Steenkamp’s book, A Mother’s Story, released in 2014 she wrote: “As long as we live, as long as breathe, Barry and I will struggle to come to terms with Reeva’s death. We are locked in unbearable grief forever.” BARRY STEENKAMP: A lot of people have said that June is this stone-faced person, does she actually feel or whatever. I know that June grieves like I do all the time. She is most probably a bit stronger, but she grieves. I hear her at night, I hear her cry. In advocate Barry Roux’s closing arguments, he argued that Judge Masipa should consider whether the threat of an attack was subjectively perceived to be real at the time of the offence. JOHN LINK: The central theme in Roux’s closing arguments is his believe that some in society still confuse dolus eventualis with dolus directus – with other words, despite the findings of the Supreme Court of Appeal, some people still mistakenly, perhaps even willfully believe that Oscar intended to shoot Reeva Steenkamp. BARRY ROUX: We say, my Lady, that as the result as a sustained campaign of misonformation, the accused’s reputation will never recover. JOHN LINK: Roux went on to argue that some members of society appears unable to reconcile their image of Oscar as the medal-winning athlete standing 1,84 metres on his blades with the anxious man standing 1,5 metres on his stumps, who on the morning of the shooting believed that his life was in danger. BARRY ROUX: Some people refuse point-black to see in context the true facts. They want to see Oscar Pistorius running to the bathroom with his gold medal around his neck. JUDGE GREENLAND: He addressed society and lambasted it and scolded it. In my 35 years in the court I’ve never seen this but I cant fault Barry for doing it. In an unexpected move, advocate Roux asked Oscar to remove his prosthetic legs. On his stumps, Oscar walked past Reeva’s family and the prosecution team and then stood in front of Judge Masipa, with his head bowed. BARRY ROUX: Let’s look at who is the person. After incorporating the Supreme Court of Appeal’s finding to view the sentence. He was suffering from an anxiety disorder, that is not gone. This must all be seen in the context of his disability and the pervasive effect of the disability on his subjective thinking. I don’t want to overplay disability, but at time has come that we must just look with different eyes, at least with unbiased eyes. MANNIE WITZ: I think the visual reminder is very important. Any prociding officer, when you actually see it, one or two minutes of actually seeing it, is better than an hour explaining it JUDGE GREENLAND: Oscar is still a human being judge Masipa has to also protect his interest, and she was put into a better position to do so by that visual impact of seeing him on his stumps. According to the Criminal Procedures Act, murder carries a minimum sentence of 15 years imprisonment unless substantial and compelling circumstances exist. MANNIE WITZ: You can just see Oscar, as this trial has progressed, look at him now, nevermind that he now faces the minimum sentence, he is a broken man BARRY ROUX: The accused has paid from the minute he fired the shots and will pay for this for the rest of his life. Roux has asked the court for a sentence of correctional supervision. Professor Scholtz testified that further imprisonment would serve no constructive purpose for Oscar. In prosecutor Gerrie Nel’s closing arguments he emphasizes that the benchmark for murder is a minimum of 15 years. GERRIE NEL: Correctional supervision is not even close to the benchmark. JOHN LINK:Nel turned immediately to an issue covered extensively by Barry Roux in his closing arguments. He acknowledged that the SCA had found Oscar guilty of murder dolus eventualis, but said this shooting was far removed from negligence. GERRIE NEL: At the time the fatal shots were fired, the possibility of death of the person behind the door was a clear and obvious result, and infiring not one, but four shots, such a result become even more likely. My Lady, more likely than obvious. My Lady, it borders on Dolus Directus, not on negligence, My Lady. JOHN LINK: Throughout sentencing, Nel referred to a television interview that Oscar had taken part in prior to these proceedings. He said in doing so, and in not choosing to testify in mitigation of sentence had shown disrespect for the court. He also accused Oscar of showing no remorse. MANNIE WITZ: The defence laid down a proper basis from the evidence of Prof Scholtz why he couldn’t actually give the evidence to express the remorse, when you give evidence in mitigation of sentence or extentuation of sentence, you can be cross-examined and you can be cross-examined on the very merits of the case. GERRIE NEL: My Lady, there is a difference: “I am very sorry that Reeva is dead,” and “I feel sorry for myself because she is dead.” That I understand. But, my Lady, why? In the light of these contradictions one really does not know what his explanation is for firing the fatal shots. My Lady, that in itself, excludes remorse. JUDGE GREENLAND: He owes the court an explanation. He owes society an explanation, he owes the Steenkamps an explanation, especially on that critical issue as to what was his intention when he fired those shots. I think the SCA has lamented the fact that is still unanswered. GERRIE NEL: Life was the most valuable asset of the deceased. My Lady, it does not matter if the accused thought she was an intruder. Is an intruder’s life not important? Did he not think of an intruder’s life? He didn’t. He intentionally, in his view, on the argument of the defence, intentionally killed an intruder. That’s not important. As long as we can just cover in our argument that he never though he was killing Reeva, then we’re covered. Prosecutor Gerrie Nel asked that Judge Masipa do not deviate from the prescribed minimum 15-year imprisonment for murder. JUDGE GREENLAND: The sentence that I would impose is one of 15 years house arrest. Where house arrest means house imprisonment. In other words no liberties except liberties within his home environment, coupled with 15 years of community service MANNIE: I think it would probably be an effective term of imprisonment in these circumstances. Judge Masipa will hand down her sentence on July, the 6th. Barry said that he believed that one day he’d be able to meet with Oscar. BARRY STEENKAMP: It’s been very difficult for me to forgive, but he has to pay for his crime. PROMO’S PROMO 1:15” BARRY STEENKAMP: People say it takes two, three years to get over something like this. But everyday of my life is the same. A broken Barry Steenkamp says Oscar Pistorius has to pay for what he’s done. PROMO 2:15” BARRY ROUX: Let’s let at who is this man – with unbiased eyes. PROF. SCHOLTZ: one would describe him as “broken”. Barry Steenkamp, a broken man himself, says Oscar must pay for what he’s done. BARRY STEENKAMP: It’s been very difficult for me to forgive. PROMO 3:10” It’s been three years and four months since Oscar Pistorius shot and killed his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp. Now convicted of murder, he was back in court this week for sentencing proceedings. This week, though, the court was given a direct insight into the “devastation” Oscar wrote about , from Reeva’s father, Barry Steenkamp. Words of loss and sympathy – written by Oscar Pistorius and posted on his website exactly one year after he shot and killed his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp on Valentine’s day 2013. But another distraught and broken man, sometimes even at a loss for words, was Reeva’s father, Barry Steenkamp, who testified in aggravation of sentence for the first time this week. But the Appeal Court also ruled that despite Oscar maintaining that he believed there was in intruder, “the identity of his victim is irrelevant to his guilt”.

metadata.Summary: This week, in the same court that Oscar Pistorius stood trial, he will have to face chief prosecutor Gerrie Nel and Judge Masipa again. Only this time, the prospect of a much longer sentence hangs over his head. During the sentencing procedure, adv Gerrie Nel will call witnesses in aqggravation of Pistorius's sentence, while adv Barry Roux will call witnesses in mitigation of his sentence.
metadata.Further information: It is not the first time that this process is being followed. In October 2014, Judge Masipa sentenced Oscar Pistorius to five years in prison according to section 276 (1)(i) of the Criminal Procedures Act - which meant that in Oscar's case he had to serve 10 months of his five year sentence - one fifth according to the section he was sentenced to. He was supposed to be released on the 21st of August last year, but Minister of Justice found a techical error in the law and he was only released in October, one year less than a year from the date he first entered the Kgosi Mampuru II prison in Pretoria. Not long after - in November 2015 - Gerrie Nel brought his application at the Supreme Court of Appeal to have Judge Masipa's verdict of culpable homicide changed to murder. And in December 2015, in an unanimous judgment - written and read by Chief Justice Eric Leach - the verdict was changed to murder - Oscar Pistorius's must have foreseen that by firing four shots through the toilet cubicle he would have killed the person behind the door and therefore he was guilty of murder. And that is why we find ourselves at the High Court in Pretoria again now - two years and three months after Oscar Pistorius's initial trial started. It is likely that court will sit the entire week - chief prosecutor Gerrie Nel and adv Barry Roux will call their respective witnesses to testify in aggravation and mitigation of his sentence and then the two legal heads still has to deliver their final arguments. It is then likely that Judge Masipa will postpone the case to deliberate her sentence.
